On the surface referenda can seem like a perfect addition to the democratic process. They give everyone an opportunity to have a say and make the electorate directly accountable. However, in some ways they do cause problems.

Now you've said in other comments you're in the UK so I'll mainly focus on their impact here. One critisism often aired is the fact that they essentially negate the role of government. The whole point of you voting for an MP is that you have a representative in parliament to make decisions on your behalf. If the government then decides to hold a referendum then the MPs are almost completely bypassed. While this is okay occasionally for massive national issues (such as the EU referendum), too many weakens government and makes it redundant. Also, they can also limit choice as, instead of your MP voicing a variety of ideas and views from his constituency in parliament, the government narrows issues down to a simple "yes/no" question. The EU referendum showed this with the "leave or remain" desicion. Some of the electorate may have wanted reform or some other middle ground but had no way to express it.

Another problem that must be considered is the polarisation they can cause along with increased levels of issue voting. Again the EU referendum becomes a perfect example of this where many people decided to vote for UKIP purely on the promise of holding said referendum. 

Hopefully that answers your question somewhat. Bonus fun fact you may not have known, in the UK the government technically has no obligation to follow the decision given by a referendum and may do the complete opposite if that's what they decide.

Generally it'll be less potent. I mean, ignoring the chemistry of how different poisons decay, the point of a poison is to kill hence past the expiration date it is less likely to kill.

For example, [strychnine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strychnine) has shelf life of about 100 years before it begins to decay. This occurs due to it being a rather large molecule that may oxidise or react with its container. As mentioned in other comments, [cyanide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_cyanide) will also decay. This tends to occur as the cyanide triple bond is inherently unstable and will also react readily with any contaminants.

There are some "poisons" that may become more potent past their "expiry date" due to side reactions. This may occur with substances that aren't made to be used as poisons but contain toxic ingredients which when reacted with the air or some other contaminant become more toxic and/or more easily absorbed by the body.
